subject: civil
audience: FE Civil candidates and civil engineering students
title: The Floor Beam That Was Loaded at 400 lb/ft, Not 50
featured_title: THE FLOOR BEAM THAT WAS LOADED AT 400 LB/FT, NOT 50

presentation.challenge: The floor load was 50 psf. The beam did not carry 50 lb/ft—it carried 400 lb/ft.

practice.primary_question: Why must an area load in psf be multiplied by tributary width before it is applied to a beam as a line load?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Applying a floor pressure in psf directly to a beam as if it were already a plf line load.

case_dna.target_misconception: A 50 psf floor load can be applied to a supporting beam as 50 lb/ft.
case_dna.why_plausible: Both are stated per foot in everyday language, but psf is force per area and plf is force per length.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With beams spaced 8 ft apart, one interior beam supports an 8 ft tributary width. The line load is 50 psf × 8 ft = 400 plf.
case_dna.corrected_model: Convert area load to line load using tributary width: w_line = q_area × tributary width.

problem_statement: An interior floor beam supports a uniform floor load of 50 psf. Adjacent beams are spaced 8 ft apart, so the beam's tributary width is 8 ft. A calculation applies 50 lb/ft directly to the beam. Determine the correct line load and identify the unit/load-path mistake.
fixed_constraints: Ignore beam self-weight for this exercise

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The pressure was correct. The beam load was not.
gates.prompt: What conversion is required before the floor load can be used in a beam analysis?

options.label: Multiply area load by tributary width to obtain line load
Use 50 psf as 50 plf because both contain 'per foot'
options.reason: The units represent different dimensions: area versus length.

options.label: Divide the area load by beam spacing
options.reason: For a tributary strip, the beam accumulates load over width, so the load is multiplied by that width.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the beam line load
gates.prompt: What uniform line load in lb/ft acts on the beam?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Aggregate the tributary strip
gates.result: The beam carries 400 lb/ft from the floor load.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the load conversion
gates.prompt: Calculate 50 psf × 8 ft. Enter the beam line load.
gates.hint: The tributary width cancels one length dimension.

cards.text: Floor loading is specified as force per area: 50 lb/ft².
The beam supports an 8 ft-wide tributary strip.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the beam-loading note
report: C1. The floor load is 50 psf.
C2. The beam spacing is 8 ft.
C3. Therefore the beam load is 50 lb/ft.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It skips the tributary-width conversion from area load to line load.

evidence_choices.label: 50 psf × 8 ft = 400 plf
evidence_choices.reason: This is the correct dimensional conversion for the tributary strip.

correction.template: The floor load produces a beam line load of {w} lb/ft.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce the beam line load without changing the floor pressure
gates.constraint: Keep the floor pressure at 50 psf.

options.label: Reduce tributary width from 8 ft to 4 ft by adding another supporting beam
Increase tributary width to 12 ft
options.reason: That increases the line load to 600 plf.

options.label: Keep 8 ft spacing but treat 50 psf as 50 plf

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply tributary-width loading
gates.prompt: A floor load is 60 psf and a beam's tributary width is 10 ft. What line load reaches the beam?

options.label: 6 lb/ft
options.reason: That divides rather than accumulates the area load.

gates.explanation: Area load multiplied by tributary width becomes line load.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the structural load path
gates.confirmation: I confirm that area loads must be converted through tributary geometry before being applied to line members.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A 50 psf floor load was applied as 50 plf.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The beam collects load across an 8 ft tributary width.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use w=q×tributary width and verify dimensions.

seo.seo_title: Tributary Area to Beam Load: Why 50 psf Becomes 400 plf | FE E-044
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil Case E-044: a 50 psf floor load over an 8 ft tributary width becomes a 400 plf beam load.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Civil tributary area beam load
seo.excerpt: A floor pressure cannot be applied directly as a beam line load. Tributary width converts psf into plf.
seo.direct_answer: For an interior beam supporting an 8 ft tributary width under a 50 psf floor load, the beam line load is 50×8=400 lb/ft. The tributary width converts force per area into force per length.

faqs.q: How do you convert psf to plf on a beam?
faqs.a: Multiply the area load by the beam's tributary width.

faqs.q: What line load comes from 50 psf over 8 ft tributary width?
